questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle
questions.worked_solution:
The velocity is the derivative of the position function $x(t)$ with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\operatorname{cot}⁡t}) \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cot}⁡t\cdot \frac{1}{t}-\operatorname{ln}⁡t(-{csc}^{2}⁡t))}{{cot}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡t+t\operatorname{ln}⁡t{csc}^{2}⁡t}{t})}{{cot}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡t+t\operatorname{ln}⁡t{csc}^{2}⁡t}{t{cot}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The position $x$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by $x(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}+1}.$ Calculate the velocity at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The velocity is the derivative of the position function $x(t)$ with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{2t({t}^{2}+1)-{t}^{2}(2t)}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{t}^{3}+2t-2{t}^{3}}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by 

$$
s(t)=4{e}^{-t}+3{t}^{2}-2t+1,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the velocity at time $t=2.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{-t}+3{t}^{2}-2t+1) \\  & =-4{e}^{-t}+6t-2\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the velocity at $t=2,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the velocity function above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =-4{e}^{-2}+6\cdot 2-2 \\  & =-4{e}^{-2}+10 \\  & =9.458\,658… \\  & ≈9.46\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The displacement $s$ (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by the equation $s(t)=(2t+1)^{3}$, where $t$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the position and velocity of the particle at the initial moment of time $t=0\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the initial position, we substitute $t=0$ it into the equation $s(t)=(2t+1)^{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{0} & =s(0) \\  & =(2\cdot 0+1)^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((2t+1)^{3}) \\  & =6(2t+1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the velocity at $t=0\,\text{s},$ we substitute $t=0$ into the velocity function above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(0) \\  & =6(2\cdot 0+1)^{2} \\  & =6(1)^{2} \\  & =6\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The displacement (in meters) of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the equation $s(t)=2{t}^{4}-3t+5$, where $t\ge 0$ is measured in seconds. At how many seconds is the particle's velocity equal to $509\,\text{m/s}?$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{4}-3t+5) \\  & =8{t}^{3}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want to know when the velocity is $509\,\text{m/s}$, we substitute $v(t)=509$ into the equation above and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}509 & =8{t}^{3}-3 \\ 512 & =8{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{3} & =\frac{512}{8} \\ {t}^{3} & =64 \\ t & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle is $509\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle when $t=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\text{s}.$ Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

The speed of the particle is approximately
{{field-1}}$\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed is $|-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}|=\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}≈2.47\,\text{m/s}$ to 2 decimal places.

$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{4}-3{t}^{2}+t) \\  & =24{t}^{3}-6t+1\end{aligned}
$$

 
To calculate the velocity at $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the velocity function above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =24(1)^{3}-6(1)+1 \\  & =24-6+1 \\  & =19\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle is $19\,\textrm{m/s}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t) = t^2 - 36t,\quad t\geq 0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle when $t=1\,\textrm{s}$.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-36t) \\  & =2t-36\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=1,$ the velocity is

$$
v(1) = 2(1) - 36 = -34.
$$

Therefore, the speed is $|{-34}| = 34\, \textrm{m/s}.$
